summary: A short 1969 note by Vint Cerf about a message of zero text length used to signal end-of-file. It shows a message layout containing a leader, a marking field, a checksum and padding. It is an early, informal protocol note.

plainLanguage.summary: When you finish reading a book you reach the last page. This note describes an empty message that tells the other computer there is no more to come.

questions: how did early arpanet signal end of file
subtitle: Vint Cerf's 1969 proposal to use a zero-length message to mark the end of a file.

tldr.problem: File transmissions over auxiliary connections needed some way to say end of file.
tldr.mechanism: Send a message whose text length is zero. Figure 1 shows its layout: a leader, a marking field, a 16-bit checksum and padding.
tldr.outcome: The note is a one-page proposal that refers back to RFC 11 and does not discuss alternatives, errors or how it is to be used beyond the layout.

sections.title: Why an End-of-File Signal
sections.content:
The proposal is written by Vint Cerf at UCLA, dated 20 August 1969, and refers to RFC 11. The author notes that file transmissions over auxiliary connections will need a mechanism to say END-OF-FILE.

The suggestion is that a message of length 0 (zero) be used for the purpose. Because every message already carries a length, a message with no text is easy to tell apart from data.
sections.plainLanguage: When the last page has been sent, send a blank page to say the book is finished.

sections.title: The Zero Text Length Message
sections.content:
Figure 1 shows the layout of the zero text length EOF message as four fields in order: a 32-bit leader, a 32-bit marking, a 16-bit checksum and padding. The figure labels the padding width with a question mark, so it is not fixed in the text.

The RFC does not explain the individual fields. It gives only the figure and the proposal.
sections.plainLanguage: The empty envelope still has an address part, a spacer, a check number and some filler, but nothing inside.

sections.title: What the Note Leaves Open
sections.content: RFC 13 is a single page. It says nothing about acknowledgements, error handling or what a receiver should do on seeing the message, and it refers only to RFC 11 for the surrounding context.
sections.plainLanguage: It is only a first idea. The author does not say what the receiver does next.

references.text: NWG/RFC 11, referred to as the source of the auxiliary-connection file transmissions.
